messages.author: a5d94cca01490293
messages.subject: Robust correlation (t-distribution) in Stan
parts:
Hi, I am trying to do robust correlations using t-distribution in stan. I found it in jags (http://www.sumsar.net/blog/2013/08/robust-bayesian-estimation-of-correlation/) but it is very slow... Do anyone have a syntax to do it? Thanks a lot.

Danilo
Brazil

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: Robust correlation (t-distribution) in Stan
parts:
Hi Danilo,

something like:


parameters {
matrix[K,J] beta;
cholesky_factor_corr[K] L_Omega;
vector<lower=0>[K] L_sigma;
real<lower=2> nu;
corr_matrix[K] Omega;


}
model {
vector[K] mu[N];
matrix[K,K] L_Sigma;
for (n in 1:N)
mu[n] <- beta * x[n];
L_Sigma <- diag_pre_multiply(L_sigma, L_Omega);
to_vector(beta) ~ normal(0, 5);
nu ~ gamma(2,0.1);
L_Omega ~ lkj_corr_cholesky(4);
L_sigma ~ cauchy(0, 2.5);
Omega <- multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L_Omega);

y ~ multi_student_t(nu, mu,Omega);

}

Not tested though. 

Andre

messages.author: 71c315ee557ff234
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Robust correlation (t-distribution) in Stan
parts:
should be:

Omega <- multiply_lower_tri_self_transpose(L_Sigma);


The idea is just lkj_corr_cholesky samples a correlation matrix in cholesky form, 
then we multiply L_sigma to L_Omega to get the cholesky form of the cov.
With L*L', where L is a chol. matrix we get the covariance matrix "back".
STAN has no cholesky form of multivariate studentt. 

Hope it helps,
Andre

This won't work because you can't assign to Omega and L_Omega
in the model block --- you can only assign in the block in
which the variable is defined. You also can't double-declare L_Sigma.
So either declare these local variables in the model and define them
there, or declare them as transformed parameters and define in that block.

RStan uses the exact same model syntax, so nothing to translate there.

- Bob

messages.author: b9804e09e21c2cc0
messages.subject: Re: Robust correlation (t-distribution) in Stan
parts:
Danilo,

I did this based on Lee and Wagenmakers (2013) correlation with Pearson Correlation With Uncertainty in Measurement and Stan's example of this model:

# clears workspace:
rm(list=ls())
graphics.off()

library(rstan)

#### Notes to Stan model #######################################################
## 1) All notes from previous model Correlation_1 also apply to this model.
## 2) If you change sigmaerror to c(0.03, 10) as suggested in excercise 5.2.2
##    warning statements will be more frequent and posterior less smooth.
################################################################################
model <- "
// Pearson Correlation With Uncertainty in Measurement
data {
int<lower=0> n;
vector[2] x[n];
vector[2] sigmaerror;
}
transformed data {
real par;
par <- 1/29.0;
}
parameters {
vector[2] mu;
vector<lower=0>[2] nuMinusOne;
vector<lower=0>[2] lambda;
real<lower=-1,upper=1> r;
vector[2] y[n];
}
transformed parameters {
vector<lower=1>[2] nu;
vector<lower=0>[2] sigma;
cov_matrix[2] T;
nu <- nuMinusOne + 1;

// Reparameterization
sigma[1] <- inv_sqrt(lambda[1]);
sigma[2] <- inv_sqrt(lambda[2]);

T[1,1] <- square(sigma[1]);
T[1,2] <- r * sigma[1] * sigma[2];
T[2,1] <- r * sigma[1] * sigma[2];
T[2,2] <- square(sigma[2]);
}
model {
// Priors
nuMinusOne ~ exponential(par);
mu ~ normal(0, inv_sqrt(.001));
lambda ~ gamma(.001, .001);
// Data
y ~ multi_normal(mu, T);
for (i in 1:n)
x[i] ~ student_t(nu, y[i], sigmaerror);
}"

# Generate fake correlated data
library(MASS)
set.seed(777)
m <- 2
b <- 50
sigma <- matrix(c(1, 0.8, 0.8, 1), nrow=2)
x <- mvrnorm(b,mu=rep(0, m),Sigma=sigma,empirical=T)

n <- nrow(x) # number of people/units measured

# precision of measurement:
sigmaerror = c(.03, 1)
# sigmaerror = c(.03, 10)

data <- list(x=x, n=n, sigmaerror=sigmaerror) # to be passed on to Stan
myinits <- list( list(r=0, mu=c(0, 0), nuMinusOne=c(4,4), lambda=c(1, 1),
                      y=matrix(c(rep(1, n), rep(100, n)), n, 2)))

# parameters to be monitored:  
parameters <- c("r", "nu", "mu", "sigma")

# The following command calls Stan with specific options.
# For a detailed description type "?rstan".
samples <- stan(model_code=model,  
                data=data,
                init=myinits,  # If not specified, gives random inits
                pars=parameters,
                iter=20000,
                chains=1,
                thin=1,
                warmup = 100,  # Stands for burn-in; Default = iter/2
                seed = 777  # Setting seed; Default is random seed
               )

# Summary of analysis
summary(samples)

It's not perfect yet, but I think it's very close to what you need.
Maybe someone else can be able to modify what is wrong.

Cheers,
Víthor Rosa Franco

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Re: Robust correlation (t-distribution) in Stan
parts:
Only to run multiple chains.

We strongly recommend against those fat inverse gamma priors
for both computational and statistical reasons. See the manual
chapter on regression for recommendations and our new Wiki:

https://github.com/stan-dev/stan/wiki/Prior-Choice-Recommendations

You're probably better off with a direct Cholesky-factor
parameterization, but if you want to create your own 2 x 2 matrix,
then instead of this

>
> T[1,2] <- r * sigma[1] * sigma[2];
> T[2,1] <- r * sigma[1] * sigma[2];

you want to reuse the element:

T[2,1] <- T[1, 2];

And you want to vectorize this the other way
around:

> for (i in 1:n)
> x[i] ~ student_t(nu, y[i], sigmaerror);
> }"

x: (n x 2)
y: (n x 2)
nu: (2 x 1)
sigmaerror: (2 x 1)

by insteading reordering

x: (2 x n)
y: (2 x n)

so you can do this:

for (k in 1:2)
x[k] ~ student_t(nu[k], y[k], sigmaerror[k]);

That vectorizes all the elements together with the same mean
and sd, which allows the relevant subexpressions to be reused.

- Bob
